Today they see his first real test at capture the flag and set it beside an ancient K'iche' Maya trial of heroes, the Hero Twins' ballgame.","enduringUnderstanding":"Cultures around the world tell stories of contests and trials to show what they admire in a hero: courage, teamwork, cleverness, and a bond with powerful forces.","futureLessons":"In Lesson 16 students read the Oracle scene in Chapter 9 and analyze what is stated and implied about Percy's future. The comparing and evidence skills practiced today carry into that lesson and into the Delphi article in the homework.","performanceTask":"The Shared Stories, Shared Lessons task asks students to compare texts, use multi-source evidence, use abstract nouns, and keep their writing cohesive. Today's paragraph is a short rehearsal of all four."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"identity","definition":"who a person truly is, including their qualities and where they come from","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"transformation","definition":"a big change in how someone or something looks, acts, or is","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"responsibility","definition":"a duty or job that a person is expected to take care of","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"fate","definition":"the events that are believed to be planned for a person by a power beyond their control","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"trial","definition":"a difficult test of a person's strength, skill, or character","tier":"support"},{"word":"supernatural","definition":"beyond what science can explain, such as gods, spirits, or magic","tier":"support"},{"word":"contest","definition":"a game or competition in which people try to win","tier":"support"},{"word":"outwit","definition":"to beat someone by being smarter or more clever","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief (Chapter 8)","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"pp. 117–126"},{"title":"Popol Vuh: the Hero Twins' ballgame and the lords of Xibalba (excerpt)","author":"K'iche' Maya sacred narrative, English translation by Lewis Spence (Project Gutenberg)","pages":"Short excerpt selected by the teacher"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Activate what students know about games with high stakes and connect today's comparison to the essential question.","activities":[{"id":"launch-turn-and-talk","title":"When a Game Is More Than a Game","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.9"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Think of a game, sport, or contest from a story, movie, or your own life where the game showed what someone was really made of. Tell your partner what happened and what it showed about that person."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What can a contest show about a person that everyday life might not?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It can show if someone stays brave when it gets hard, or if they can work with a team. In my soccer game, our goalie got hurt and kept playing, and that showed how tough she is."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Today you will look at two contests from two cultures: Percy's capture-the-flag game in Chapter 8, and the ballgame the Hero Twins play against the lords of Xibalba in the Popol Vuh. Then you will write about what each contest shows about being a hero."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Prep before class: choose and print one short excerpt of the Hero Twins' ballgame and trials in Xibalba from the Lewis Spence translation on Project Gutenberg (about one to two pages). Students should be able to identify the ball playing that disturbs the lords, the trials in the dark, cold, jaguar, fire, and bat houses, the tricks the twins use, and the final ballgame. Check the sample responses below against your excerpt and adjust details if your excerpt differs."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Teach pronouns in the proper case, then show how verbs and adjectives become abstract nouns that sharpen analysis.","activities":[{"id":"lab-pronoun-case","title":"Pronouns in the Proper Case","minutes":6,"standards":["L.6.1","L.6.1.a"],"routine":"Language Study","blocks":[{"type":"teach","text":"hh"},{"type":"directions","text":"Read the sentences. Decide whether each underlined pronoun is the doer of the action (subjective), the receiver of the action (objective), or shows ownership (possessive). Then fix any pronoun that is in the wrong case."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Pronouns change form depending on their job. Subjective pronouns (I, he, she, we, they) do the action. Objective pronouns (me, him, her, us, them) receive the action or follow a preposition. Possessive pronouns (my, his, her, our, their) show ownership. In compare-and-contrast writing you will often name two characters at once, so check your case."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Model sentence 1: Annabeth gave Percy a plan, and him guarded the creek. Model sentence 2: Chiron saw the trident above Percy's head and spoke to he. Model sentence 3: The twins fooled the lords with their tricks."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"In sentence 1, who is guarding the creek, and what pronoun should do that action?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy is doing the guarding, so it is the doer. It should be the subjective pronoun *he*: 'and he guarded the creek.'"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"In sentence 2, what is the pronoun doing, and how do we fix it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It comes after the word *to*, so it receives the action. It should be the objective pronoun *him*: 'spoke to him.'"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"In sentence 3, what kind of pronoun is *their*, and how do you know?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It is possessive because it shows the tricks belong to the twins. The sentence is already correct."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Here is a quick trick for two subjects: take one person out. You would never say 'Him guarded the creek,' so you would not say 'Annabeth and him guarded the creek.' You would say 'Annabeth and he guarded the creek.'"},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help English learners notice the three jobs pronouns do and practice choosing the correct form in speaking before writing.","sayAsk":"Say: Point to who does the action. Ask: Who is doing the action? Who gets the action? Provide frames: ___ (he/she/they) guarded the creek. Chiron spoke to ___ (him/her/them). That trick was ___ (his/her/their) idea. Invite students to say the corrected sentence aloud twice with a partner.","watchFor":"If students choose *him* for the doer, then have them remove the second name and say the sentence again. If students mix up *their* and *they*, then ask: Does it show ownership or do the action? Success looks like students naming the pronoun's job and correcting one sentence aloud."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: choosing between subjective and objective pronouns","tryThis":"Give a three-column anchor chart (Doer, Receiver, Owner) with example pronouns. Have students try the 'take one person out' test on each sentence before writing."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Have students write one sentence about Percy and Annabeth together and one about the Hero Twins together, using a subjective pronoun in one and an objective pronoun in the other, then label each."}]}]},{"id":"lab-abstract-nouns","title":"From Verbs and Adjectives to Abstract Nouns","minutes":4,"standards":["L.6.6","L.6.3"],"routine":"Word Study","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Strong analytical writers turn actions and describing words into idea words. The adjective *brave* becomes the noun *courage*. The verb *transform* becomes *transformation*. The adjective *responsible* becomes *responsibility*. Notice the endings: *-tion*, *-ity*, *-ness*, and sometimes a new word altogether. These nouns let you name an idea and then explain it."},{"type":"directions","text":"With a partner, turn each word into an abstract noun, then finish the sentence frame: clever → ___ ; brave → ___ ; transform → ___ ; responsible → ___ . Frame: Percy's trial shows ___ because ___."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which sounds more like analysis: 'Percy was brave' or 'Percy's courage is tested'? Why?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"'Percy's courage is tested' sounds more like analysis because it names the idea, courage, and then I can explain how it is tested. 'Percy was brave' just describes him."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Expected answers: clever → cleverness, brave → courage (not bravery only; accept both), transform → transformation, responsible → responsibility. Tell students that *identity* and *fate* are already abstract nouns they will use in their paragraphs."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Keep these nouns handy. In a few minutes you will use at least one of them in your comparison paragraph."}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Part A: Cite moments from Chapter 8 to show what Percy's trial reveals about his abilities and identity (RL.6.1). Part B: Cite moments from the Popol Vuh excerpt to show what kind of heroes the twins are (RL.6.1, W.6.9). Part C: Compare the two contests (W.6.9). Part D: Draft a comparison paragraph with evidence from both texts and pronouns in the proper case (W.6.9, L.6.1.a).","activities":[{"id":"lia-percy-evidence","title":"Part A: Percy's Trial at Capture the Flag","minutes":8,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.3"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 8","pages":"pp. 117–126"},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread pp. 117–126. Annotate three moments: (1) Percy's strategy in the creek, (2) the injury, and (3) the trident appearing above his head. In your notes, write what happens in each moment and what it shows about Percy's abilities or identity."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What happens to Percy at the creek and after he is injured, and what does that show about him?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy guards the creek and gets hurt in the fight, but the water heals him and makes him stronger. That shows he has an ability connected to water that he did not know about, which hints at who he really is."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does the trident appearing above his head tell us, and how do you know?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It tells us he is a son of Poseidon. The trident shows up right after he proves his power in the fight and the hellhound attack, and the characters react like it is a sign from a god."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Push for evidence, not just retelling. Have students point to the page where each moment happens and use phrases like 'On page ___, Percy ___, which shows ___.' Keep all evidence from pp. 117–126."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.1"],"stem":"In Chapter 8, what does the water in the creek help show about Percy?","choices":[{"text":"The water heals and strengthens him, showing a power linked to his true identity.","correct":true,"rationale":"This is correct. The creek restores Percy during the fight, and this helps lead to the trident sign that reveals he is a son of Poseidon."},{"text":"The creek is only a place to hide from Clarisse and her team.","correct":false,"rationale":"Percy does use the creek as part of his strategy, but the text shows the water does more than hide him; it heals and strengthens him."},{"text":"The water shows that Percy is not a good fighter and needs help from Annabeth.","correct":false,"rationale":"Percy is injured, but the water gives him power, so the scene reveals ability, not weakness."},{"text":"The creek shows that the camp rules forbid Percy from using weapons.","correct":false,"rationale":"The text does not say this. It focuses on the water's effect on Percy."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in explaining sequence and cause in the capture-the-flag scene using adverbials of time, place, and cause (ELD.PII.6.5).","sayAsk":"Say: Tell your partner what happened to Percy and where. Provide frames: At the creek, Percy ___. After the injury, the water ___. Because the trident appeared above his head, everyone ___. Encourage students to add a place phrase (in the creek, above his head) and a cause phrase (because, after).","watchFor":"If students only retell the game, then ask: What does this moment show about Percy? If students give no detail, then point to a specific paragraph and ask what happens there. Success looks like a sentence with an event, a detail phrase, and an explanation of what it shows."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: choosing which moments matter","tryThis":"Give a three-box organizer (Creek, Injury, Trident) and have students write one sentence of what happens and one sentence of what it shows in each box."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to explain how the hellhound attack and the trident sign together shape what the other campers think of Percy."}]}]},{"id":"lia-twins-evidence","title":"Part B: The Hero Twins' Ballgame","minutes":7,"standards":["RL.6.1","W.6.9"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"Popol Vuh: the Hero Twins' ballgame and the lords of Xibalba (excerpt, Lewis Spence translation)","pages":"Teacher-selected excerpt"},{"type":"directions","text":"Read the Popol Vuh excerpt. Annotate three moments: how the twins play, a trap or trial they face in Xibalba, and a way they outwit the lords. Write what happens and what it shows about what kind of heroes the twins are."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What trials do the Hero Twins face, and how do they handle them?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The lords of Xibalba, who are angry about the twins' noisy ball playing, send them through dangerous houses. The twins survive by using tricks, like fooling the lords with fake lights, so they are clever, not just strong."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does the ballgame show about the twins' relationship to powerful forces?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The twins face the lords of the underworld, who are very powerful and dangerous. The game becomes a test of whether the twins can stand up to the gods of death, and it shows they have a special connection to that world."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Because the excerpt is teacher-selected, tie responses to what your excerpt actually says. Students should paraphrase or quote briefly from the excerpt and name it as the Popol Vuh. Remind students that the Popol Vuh is a sacred story of the K'iche' Maya, so we treat it as a story with real meaning to a culture, not just 'a myth.'"},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.1"],"stem":"In the Popol Vuh excerpt, how do the Hero Twins mainly succeed against the lords of Xibalba?","choices":[{"text":"They use cleverness and tricks to outwit the lords' traps.","correct":true,"rationale":"This is correct. The twins pass trials by fooling the lords and avoiding their traps, which shows cleverness as a hero's strength."},{"text":"They win by being stronger than every lord in a fight.","correct":false,"rationale":"The twins face dangerous trials, but the text shows them winning through tricks, not brute strength."},{"text":"They avoid the lords completely and never enter Xibalba.","correct":false,"rationale":"The twins go to Xibalba and face the lords' trials, so this is not accurate."},{"text":"They are helped by a camp counselor who tells them the plan.","correct":false,"rationale":"This confuses the Popol Vuh with The Lightning Thief. In the excerpt the twins rely on their own cleverness and teamwork."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students explain what the twins do and what kind of heroes they are, evaluating the author's word choices (ELD.PI.6.7).","sayAsk":"Say: Find one word or phrase in the excerpt that shows the lords are dangerous or the twins are clever. Tell your partner why it works. Provide frames: The word ___ shows that the lords are ___. The twins are ___ because they ___. This detail shows ___.","watchFor":"If students only name events, then ask: What does this show about the twins? If students struggle with older English, then read the sentence aloud and have them restate it in everyday words. Success looks like a precise word or phrase tied to an explanation of the twins' character."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: understanding the older translation","tryThis":"Read a short passage aloud together, then have students restate each sentence in plain words before annotating. Provide a mini glossary for unfamiliar names."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to explain how the twins' trials show teamwork, since they face them as a pair, and how that compares to Percy having Annabeth's plan."}]}]},{"id":"lia-compare-chart","title":"Part C: Comparing the Two Contests","minutes":5,"standards":["W.6.9","RL.6.9"],"routine":"Think-Pair-Share","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Make a two-column chart. In the left column, write Percy's capture-the-flag trial. In the right column, write the Hero Twins' ballgame. Then add rows for: How the contest tests the hero, What it shows about courage, skill, or cleverness, The connection to powerful forces, and How it moves the plot. Fill in at least one piece of evidence for each text in each row."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What is the same in both stories, and what is different?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In both, a contest tests the hero and shows a link to powerful beings, like Poseidon or the lords of Xibalba. They are different because Percy wins through a power he just discovered, and the twins win mostly through cleverness and tricks."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Use words like *both*, *similarly*, *however*, *while*, and *in contrast* when you write. They tell the reader whether you are showing a similarity or a difference."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Give students language for comparing and contrasting with adverbials and connectors (ELD.PII.6.5, ELD.PI.6.10).","sayAsk":"Say: Compare the two trials aloud with your partner before writing. Provide frames: Both Percy and the Hero Twins ___. Similarly, ___. However, Percy ___ while the twins ___. In contrast, ___.","watchFor":"If students list facts about each story separately, then ask: How are they alike? How are they different? If students overuse *and*, then offer *similarly* and *however*. Success looks like at least one similarity and one difference stated with a connector."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: finding similarities","tryThis":"Ask guiding questions: Who tests the hero? What does the hero risk? What power is connected to the hero? Have students answer for each story in the chart."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"placeholder"}]}]},{"id":"lia-draft-paragraph","title":"Part D: Draft a Comparison Paragraph","minutes":10,"standards":["W.6.9","L.6.1","L.6.1.a","W.6.2"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"hh"}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"","keyActivities":[],"vocabularyTaught":[],"standardsCovered":[]}}
